It's December and the streets are icy. Ludwig slipped on the pavement when he went out with Fritz. Mara, who was just coming off her night shift, takes him to A&E at her hospital. Dr Yılmaz examines him.
Good morning, Mr Brandt. What happened?
I slipped on the ice. In front of the bakery. Seventy-eight years without an accident, and now this!
My right hand. The wrist. And my back hurts a bit too.
Can you move your fingers? … Good. We need to X-ray your wrist.
I'll take him to X-ray. Come on, Ludwig.
Right, Mr Brandt, here's the image. The wrist is broken, but only slightly. You'll get a plaster cast. Six weeks.
Six weeks! And Christmas? I have to cook! The whole family is coming!
You're allowed to cook, but only with your left hand. You mustn't carry anything heavy, and you shouldn't go out on your own while it's icy.
And Fritz? He has to be walked three times a day!
Don't worry. We'll find a solution. The whole house will help.
Here's a prescription for painkillers. You don't have to take them every day, only when you're in pain. Get well soon, Mr Brandt!
Thank you, doctor. But I'll tell you one thing: I'm still playing the guitar!
worries (“Mach dir keine Sorgen” = don't worry)
“müssen” has a short “ü”. “ich muss” has a short “u” (as in “put”). The difference matters: muss / müssen.
Bauch = “baukh” (a harsh “ch” after au, as in Scottish “loch”). “ck” = a short “k”: Rücken = “RÜ-ken”.
Zahn → Zähne: the “a” becomes “ä” in the plural, like a long open “e” (as in “air”).
There are two ways to say what hurts:
Ich habe Kopfschmerzen / Halsschmerzen / Bauchschmerzen / Rückenschmerzen.
I have a headache / a sore throat / stomach ache / backache.
I have a temperature / a cough / a cold.
At the doctor's in Germany you need your health insurance card (die Krankenversicherungskarte). If you miss work, the doctor gives you a sick note: die Krankschreibung (“der gelbe Schein”).
“müssen” = it's necessary, compulsory. “dürfen” = you're allowed (permission). “sollen” = someone tells you / recommends (the doctor, the boss, the law).
I have to go to the doctor. (With modals, “gehen” can be left out!)
May I smoke here? — No, you're not allowed to here.
The doctor says I should drink a lot.
3. The trap: muss nicht ≠ darf nicht
Sie müssen die Tabletten nicht nehmen.
You don't (necessarily) have to take the tablets.

“Du musst nicht kommen” = you don't need to come (you can if you want). “Du darfst nicht kommen” = I forbid you to come! In English “you must not” sounds like “musst nicht”, but it means “darf nicht”, so be careful: “muss nicht” = don't have to.

The Goethe-Zertifikat A1 exam (“Start Deutsch 1”) has four parts: listening, reading, writing (a form and a short message) and speaking (you introduce yourself, ask questions, ask for something). With these 12 chapters you're ready for it.
I have to go to the doctor today.
Am I allowed to park here?

“Sie müssen die Tabletten nicht jeden Tag nehmen” means:
You're forbidden to take them every day.
It's not necessary to take them every day.

Gestern ich bin nach Potsdam gefahren.

Wie lange muss Ludwig den Gips tragen?
Ludwig is in plaster, and the whole house has a plan. Mara has hung it on Ludwig's door, like a shift rota at the hospital.

At seven in the morning, Lena takes Fritz out before she opens the bakery. At lunchtime Ola and Kuba come, the twins from the second floor. They're allowed to hold Fritz's lead, but only together, and they have to be back before dinner. Fritz never runs as fast as he does with the twins.

In the evening Mara takes Fritz out, when she's not on the night shift. When she is on the night shift, Piotr Nowak takes him. He says he doesn't like dogs. But every evening he brings Fritz a piece of sausage.

Ludwig isn't allowed to do much, and he doesn't like that at all. He sits under his yellow lamp and complains: “I'm not ill! I've just got a broken hand!” But he has to admit it: he hasn't had so many visitors in years.

Kasia Nowak brings him pierogi. Lena brings him rolls and cakes. Mara takes his blood pressure every other day and tells him news from the ward: Mr Schulz is back home, and Jonas wants to propose to Clara on New Year's Eve. That's a secret, of course. Ludwig only tells Fritz.

The twenty-fourth of December is Christmas Eve. In the afternoon Sabine arrives from Potsdam and Thomas with his family from Munich. The flat is full. Twelve people, twelve plates, one dog. As always.
No, not as always. This year Ludwig has invited two more guests. Mara is the first. She can't fly to Sibiu, she has to work on the twenty-fifth. And the second?
At five o'clock, Mara knocks on the door on the fourth floor. Mrs Hoffmann is sitting on a chair in the hall, already dressed, with a hat and gloves, as if before a concert.
Mara, child, I don't know. Three floors. I haven't been down those stairs for two years.
We don't have to go fast. We can go as slowly as you like. One step, one break. I'm a nurse, I'll hold you.

It takes them twenty minutes. On the second floor, Ola and Kuba open the door and clap. On the first floor, the whole Brandt family is waiting in the hall. And when Mrs Hoffmann steps down the last stair, someone in the flat plays “Silent Night” on the guitar. With three fingers of the left hand, slowly and a little out of tune.
Margarete! Welcome! Forgive the wrong notes. The doctor says I'm not allowed to play with my right hand.
Ludwig Brandt, you played out of tune in 1971 too. I was at your concert in the cellar. Ingrid was standing next to me, with her book.
For a moment there's complete silence. Then Ludwig laughs, so loudly that Fritz barks. And everyone laughs.

Later, after the goose, red cabbage, dumplings and Lena's Stollen, Mara sits down by the window. It's snowing outside. The chestnut tree in the courtyard is white. On her phone there's a message from her mum: a photo of the Christmas tree in Sibiu and three words: “We miss you.”

Mara replies, for the first time in German: “I miss you too. But don't worry. I'm not alone. I've found a family here.” Then she takes a photo: twelve people, fourteen plates, one dog and a pianist at the table. And she sends it home.
Wer geht mittags mit Fritz raus?
Was will Jonas zu Silvester machen?
Warum fliegt Mara nicht nach Sibiu?
Sie hat Angst vor dem Fliegen.
Sie hat in Ludwigs Band gespielt.
